content.title: About
content.content: Toasted French or Vienna bread is a crisp slice of either whole‑grain or white loaf, achieved by a short high‑heat treatment. It features a golden crust, a characteristic aroma of caramelised starches, and a light sweetness while retaining a soft interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: French baguettes and Viennese loaves undergo longer fermentation, giving them a more pronounced flavor.
Toasted bread is traditionally used in Europe as a base for open‑face sandwiches, crostini, and soup croutons.
Toasting enhances aromatic compounds such as 2‑acetyl‑1‑pyrroline and caramelised sugars.
In many countries toasted bread with butter and garlic is served as “bruschetta”.
The crunchy crust forms through the Maillard reaction, which occurs above 150 °C.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Bread provides a steady release of energy, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, riboflavin and niacin in bread support metabolic processes.

items.title: Rich in fiber (especially whole‑grain versions)
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium and phosphorus in bread contribute to blood health and bone strength.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Toasted bread contains virtually no fat unless butter or spreads are added.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid traditional wheat bread.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Toasting can slightly raise the glycemic index, which is relevant for diabetics.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Some breads contain added salt and preservatives; choose additive‑free options when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toasted bread works well for sandwiches, as a base for pâtés, avocado, cheese, or as soup croutons. Sprinkle with herbs, garlic butter, or grated cheese and finish under the broiler for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep toasted bread in a dry container or paper bag at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze slices in a sealed bag and re‑toast in a toaster before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Doughnut holes are small, round pieces of dough made from the same yeasted or cake batter as regular doughnuts. They are typically deep‑fried until golden and finished with powdered sugar, glaze, or sprinkles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Often called “donut holes” because they look like the missing center of a traditional doughnut.
In the United States they are a popular snack at fairs and coffee shops, sometimes called “mini‑donuts.”
Both sweet and savory versions exist; savory batches are flavored with spices such as cinnamon and nutmeg.
In some countries they are used as a base for dessert salads mixed with fruit and whipped cream.
Their bite‑size shape makes them easy to pack in single‑serve bags, a favorite among kids.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Provides quick‑digesting carbohydrates that replenish muscle glycogen.

items.title: Contains some protein
items.content: The wheat‑based dough supplies a modest amount of plant protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeasted dough is a source of B1, B2, and B6 vitamins, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides small amounts of iron, magnesium, and phosphorus.

items.title: Mood‑boosting pleasure
items.content: Sweet taste can trigger endorphin release, improving mood temporarily.

items.title: High sugar and fat content
items.content: Frequent consumption may contribute to weight gain and elevated blood sugar levels.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Made with wheat flour, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Trans fats from frying
items.content: Using reused oil can introduce trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Burn risk
items.content: When frying at home, handle hot oil carefully to avoid burns.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve doughnut holes warm, dusted with powdered sugar, glaze, cinnamon, or chocolate. They pair well with berry sauce, ice cream, or can be layered in dessert parfaits.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate up to a week or freeze for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: The egg white sandwich with meat is a light meal consisting of whole‑grain bread, fluffy egg white, lean boiled or baked meat (such as turkey or chicken) and fresh vegetables. It is high in protein, low in calories and suitable for diets focused on maintaining muscle mass.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white is almost pure protein without fat or cholesterol.
Protein‑rich sandwiches are popular among athletes and people watching their figure.
Combining protein with complex carbs from whole‑grain bread provides lasting satiety.
Adding vegetables boosts vitamin and fiber content.
Preparing the sandwich at home allows control over salt and additives.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Egg white and meat together supply a complete set of amino acids that support muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: The absence of yolk and the use of lean meat make the sandwich suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole‑grain bread provide vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Selenium in egg white and zinc in meat help maintain a healthy immune system.

items.title: Fiber source
items.content: Whole‑grain bread adds dietary fiber, improving digestion and stabilizing blood sugar levels.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to egg white and should avoid the product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared meats or sauces can be high in salt; choose unseasoned lean meat and add salt sparingly.

items.title: Bacterial risk
items.content: Egg whites must be fully cooked to eliminate the risk of salmonella.

items.title: Processed bread
items.content: Some breads contain preservatives and additives; opt for whole‑grain varieties without artificial ingredients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich warm, lightly toasting the bread until golden. Add lettuce, tomato, cucumber or avocado for extra flavor and nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The assembled sandwich can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. For longer storage, keep the components separate and assemble just before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Eggplant and meat casserole is a layered dish where sautéed eggplant slices alternate with ground beef or pork, are covered with tomato sauce and baked until a golden crust forms. The eggplant adds a tender, slightly sweet flavor, while the meat provides a rich protein component.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggplant has been cultivated in the Mediterranean for over 4,000 years.
A similar dish called "imam bayıldı" appears in Ottoman cuisine, though traditionally it is vegetarian.
The combination of eggplant and meat is common in Middle Eastern and Balkan recipes.
Baking reduces the natural bitterness of eggplant and creates a creamy texture.
The casserole can be prepared ahead of time and reheated, making it popular for family meals.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat component supplies high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Eggplant is low in carbs, making the dish suitable for low‑carb eating patterns.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from eggplant supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both meat and eggplant provide B6 and B12 vitamins, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Eggplant is rich in nasunin, an anthocyanin that acts as an antioxidant and protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Using fatty ground meat or adding a lot of cheese can make the casserole calorie‑dense and high in saturated fat.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have allergies or intolerances to certain types of meat.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Tomato sauce and seasonings often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Eggplant sensitivity
items.content: Eggplant contains solanine, which can cause stomach discomfort in sensitive people; salting and rinsing slices beforehand helps reduce it.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the casserole hot as a main course, cut into portions. It pairs well with a light salad, rice, or couscous. Leftovers reheat well in the microwave or oven.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the casserole to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container. Store in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

fried-stuffed-potatoes-puerto-rican-styl.title: Fried Stuffed Potatoes, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Fried stuffed potatoes, Puerto Rican style are bite‑size potato croquettes filled with a savory mixture of meat, cheese, spices and sometimes beans. The potatoes are boiled, halved, stuffed, coated in flour and breadcrumbs, then deep‑fried until golden and crisp. The dish is a popular street snack and a staple of family meals in Puerto Rico.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the early 20th century as a way to use leftover boiled potatoes.
Traditional filling often includes “mofongo”‑style pork, tomatoes, olives, capers and aromatic herbs.
In Puerto Rico they are called “papas rellenas” (stuffed potatoes).
They are commonly served with a garlic‑avocado sauce or a tangy tomato‑based “mojo” sauce.
Variations may feature seafood, feta cheese, or a sweet version with bananas and cinnamon.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Potatoes provide steady energy and help maintain blood‑sugar levels when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports immune function and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids blood‑pressure regulation and muscle function.

items.title: Protein from meat filling
items.content: The meat adds complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Potatoes and spices such as paprika and oregano provide antioxidants that combat free radicals.

items.title: High fat from frying
items.content: Deep‑frying increases calorie density and can raise cholesterol levels if consumed excessively.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: If the filling contains shrimp or fish, people with shellfish allergies should avoid it.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt and sauces can contribute significant sodium, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Risk of overeating
items.content: The crunchy texture and rich flavor may lead to rapid overconsumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a snack or part of a main meal. Eat them with your hands, accompanied by mojo sauce, salsa, or guacamole. Pair with a fresh green salad to add balance.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked croquettes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or air‑fryer to retain crispness. Freeze in a single layer, then bag them; they keep well for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit, chocolate covered are fresh fruits dipped in a thin layer of milk or dark chocolate. They combine the natural sweetness and aroma of the fruit with the rich flavor of chocolate, creating a convenient and tasty snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chocolate‑covered fruits are popular in Europe and Asia as festive desserts.
The coating uses chocolate tempered at low temperature to keep the fruit’s shape and texture.
Common fruits used include strawberry, banana, kiwi, pineapple and grapes.
The chocolate layer protects the fruit from oxidation, extending shelf life.
Some recipes add nuts or coconut flakes for extra crunch.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fruits are rich in vitamin C, potassium and other micronutrients, while chocolate adds small amounts of magnesium and iron.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate contains flavonoids that may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of fruit sugars and chocolate fats provides a quick and sustained energy source.

items.title: Chocolate allergy
items.content: People allergic to cocoa or dairy may experience reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Chocolate‑covered fruits can be calorie‑dense and high in sugar, so consume them in moderation.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Dark chocolate contains small amounts of caffeine, which may affect sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chocolate‑covered fruits are easy to eat as a snack, add to dessert platters, use in baking, or garnish cocktails. Keep them chilled before serving to prevent the chocolate from melting.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store chocolate‑covered fruits in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑5 °C. Avoid direct sunlight and high humidity to keep the chocolate solid and the fruit fresh.

content.title: About
content.content: Gordita is a traditional Mexican dish consisting of a thin corn‑maize dough pocket filled with seasoned meat (usually beef, pork or chicken), spices and sometimes vegetables. The dough is made from masa harina, water and salt, shaped into small flat discs, stuffed and then grilled or pan‑fried until lightly crisp.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name "gordita" comes from the Spanish word for "fat" or "chubby", although the final product is usually fairly thin.
In Mexico gorditas are a popular street‑food item, often served with salsa, guacamole and a squeeze of lime.
The dough is traditionally unleavened, giving the gordita a soft, slightly chewy texture.
There are many filling variations, from classic beef to vegetarian options with beans or tofu.
Gorditas are sometimes used as a substitute for tortillas in burritos and tacos.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef and pork are good sources of heme iron, which supports normal blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat supplies B12, B6 and niacin, nutrients important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Low in simple carbs
items.content: Corn‑maize dough contains relatively few simple sugars, making gorditas suitable for moderate low‑carb diets.

items.title: Adds fiber when vegetables are included
items.content: Adding vegetables to the filling boosts dietary fiber, which aids digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Seasonings and sauces used in the filling can be salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Fatty meat options
items.content: Some fillings use fattier cuts, increasing calories and saturated fat.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: The masa dough may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to corn.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogens; ensure the filling reaches a safe internal temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve gorditas hot, split them open and top with salsa, guacamole, sour cream or fresh lime. They are handheld snacks, but can also be sliced and added to salads, bowls or burritos.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked gorditas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. They can be frozen for up to a month; reheat in the oven or skillet before serving to retain a soft texture.

infant-formula-similac-isomil-soy-powder.title: Infant formula, Similac Isomil Soy, powder, made with baby water

content.title: About
content.content: Similac Isomil Soy is a soy‑based infant formula powder designed for babies who are lactose intolerant or have a cow‑milk protein allergy. It provides plant protein, essential vitamins and minerals, and is prepared with specially treated baby water for added purity and safety.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The formula is completely plant‑based and contains no cow’s milk.
Formulated to support immune health and gentle digestion in infants with sensitive stomachs.
Includes DHA and ARA, important fatty acids for brain and eye development.
Each package comes with instructions for preparation using baby water, reducing contamination risk.
Similac Isomil Soy has undergone clinical testing confirming its safety and efficacy.

items.title: Supports growth
items.content: Provides a balanced mix of protein, fat, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals needed for normal infant growth and development.

items.title: Gentle on digestion
items.content: Soy protein is easier to digest for babies with lactose intolerance, helping to reduce colic and constipation.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A, C, D and zinc help strengthen the infant’s immune system.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: Added DHA and ARA contribute to the development of the nervous system and visual function.

items.title: Reduced risk of cow‑milk allergy
items.content: Absence of cow‑milk protein lowers the chance of allergic reactions in susceptible infants.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some infants may be allergic to soy proteins; discontinue use if symptoms appear.

items.title: Not a substitute for breastfeeding
items.content: Intended as a supplement or alternative only when breastfeeding is not possible.

items.title: Proper preparation required
items.content: Incorrect water‑to‑powder ratio can lead to hyper‑ or hypoglycemia.

items.title: Storage considerations
items.content: After opening, keep the container in a dry, cool place and use within the stated period.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Measure the recommended amount of powder, add the appropriate volume of pre‑boiled and cooled baby water (e.g., 1 scoop per 30 ml), and mix thoroughly until smooth. Use the prepared feed immediately and do not leave it at room temperature for more than 1 hour.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened container in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, use within 30 days and discard if the formula develops an off‑odor or changes color.

pan-dulce-with-fruit-no-frosting.title: Pan Dulce with Fruit, No Frosting

content.title: About
content.content: Pan Dulce is a traditional Mexican sweet bread made from a soft, yeasted dough. This version incorporates fresh fruit pieces (such as strawberry, kiwi or mango) and omits any frosting, resulting in a lighter, less sweet treat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pan Dulce originated in Mexico in the 19th century and quickly became a holiday staple.
Traditional recipes often include cinnamon, vanilla and orange zest, but this variant focuses on a fruit filling.
Fruit versions are frequently served chilled to preserve the freshness and aroma of the berries.
Skipping the frosting makes the product more suitable for those watching sugar intake.
The dough is made with flour, eggs, butter and milk, giving it a tender crumb.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: The fresh fruit adds vitamin C, vitamin A and folate, which support immune function.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fruit and whole‑grain flour contribute dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: Without frosting, the amount of added simple sugars is reduced, beneficial for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Butter provides monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from flour and fruit deliver quick and sustained energy.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Standard flour contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: Certain fruits may cause allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Natural fruit sugars
items.content: Even without frosting, fruits contain natural sugars, which should be considered by diabetics.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Butter and eggs make the product calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pan Dulce with fruit can be enjoyed as a standalone dessert, sliced into bite‑size pieces and paired with yogurt, ice cream or fresh juice. It also makes a convenient on‑the‑go snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer shelf life keep refrigerated for up to 5 days or freeze wrapped tightly in plastic.

potato-canned-fat-added-ns-as-to-fat-typ.title: Potato, canned, fat added, NS as to fat type

content.title: About
content.content: Canned potato with added fat is a ready‑to‑eat product obtained by boiling or steaming potatoes and then preserving them in oil or with added vegetable fat. It is often used as a quick side dish or an ingredient in various recipes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canning allows the potatoes to be stored for 2‑3 years without refrigeration.
Added fat enhances flavor and increases the caloric value of the product.
In some countries, canned potatoes with oil are a traditional field‑rations food for hikers and military personnel.
Canned potatoes are frequently seasoned with salt and spices to boost taste.
The technology for canning potatoes was developed in the early 20th century.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The combination of fat and carbohydrates provides a quick source of energy, especially useful in limited‑food situations.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Potatoes retain vitamin B6 and niacin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Canned potatoes contain potassium, supporting normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Thermal processing makes the potatoes soft and easy to digest, suitable for people with chewing difficulties.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Frequent consumption may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Canned products often contain significant amounts of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oils
items.content: Some individuals may react to the oils used in the product.

items.title: Bacterial contamination if the can is damaged
items.content: Compromised packaging can allow pathogenic bacteria to grow.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned potatoes can be eaten cold in salads, heated in the microwave, or added to soups, stews and casseroles. They are convenient to dice and use as a base for quick meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer the contents to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for no more than 3‑4 days.
